title: The two sons
hookLine: one brother's offering is accepted, the other kills him, and a crow shows him how to bury the body (5:27–31)
carry: one life is like all lives
last: TAWBAH — WE WRONGED OURSELVES; FORGIVE US.

cards: Sibling rivalry has its classics: who got the bigger slice, who Mom liked better, who got the car.
All week, the first human story happened between God and the first two people: a steward announced, the names, the one who wouldn't bow, a garden with one tree, a whisper, and a way back.
Now the story comes down to earth, and the very next thing it shows is a family. Two brothers. This time, the rivalry doesn't end in a slammed door.
It ends in the first death in the human story.

teach.b: Surah five tells it, and calls them simply the two sons of Adam. It never names them; tradition calls them Qabil and Habil, Cain and Abel. Each brings an offering to God.
One is accepted. The other isn't. And the one whose offering was refused says: I will kill you.
His brother's answer, in Pickthall's words: “Allah accepteth only from those who ward off (evil).” It isn't about me. Look at your own heart.
Even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won't raise mine to kill you; I fear God. His brother kills him anyway. The killer stands over the body and doesn't know what to do.
God sends a crow, scratching at the ground, to show him how to hide his brother's body. And he cries out: woe to me, can't I even be like this crow? And he's filled with regret.
Right after this story comes a line addressed to the Children of Israel.
Whoever kills a soul, except in justice, it's as if he killed all people, and in Pickthall's words, “whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.”

teach.h: ONE LIFE IS LIKE ALL LIVES.
teach.b: Jewish readers will recognize a close teaching in the Mishnah. A hadith in Bukhari adds: for every unjust killing since, a share falls on that first son, because he was the first to do it.
So the lesson of this first family is simple and enormous. One person is a whole world.

how: Muslims often cite 5:32 to teach the sanctity of every human life, and it appears in sermons and statements against violence; the story of the two sons is taught as a warning about jealousy.

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an names the two brothers
it calls them the two sons of Adam. the names Qabil and Habil come from tradition.
the murdered brother threatened to fight back
he said: even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won't raise mine to kill you.
the verse says saving one life is like saving all mankind
"whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind." (5:32)

games.q: your brother, furious that God accepted your offering and not his, says: I will kill you. what do you answer?
o: even if you raise your hand, I won't raise mine.
games.why: God accepts only from those who guard against evil, he says, and he won't raise his hand. the story honors him for it.

practice: Let a jealousy come to mind, one you've carried for a while, toward a sibling, a friend, a colleague, someone who seemed to get what you wanted; don't push it away or feed it, just notice where it lives in your body.
Then picture the other person as a whole world, with their own worries, their own sleepless nights, people who love them, and hold that for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Habil, the brother whose offering was accepted and who told Qabil it isn't about me, look at your own heart, before the first death in the human story.

orig.note: Arabic: "the two sons of Adam," the Qur'an's only name for them in 5:27.
